topic: The Hidden Geometry of Counting: From Ternary Logic to Sierpinski Fractals
target_audience: University students (Computer Science or Mathematics majors)

sections.title: The Ternary Bridge (Prerequisite Concept)
sections.content: Introduce the base-3 (ternary) numbering system as the foundation. Contrast it with binary to explain how ternary 'digits' (0, 1, 2) naturally represent three-way branching paths or three-peg systems.
sections.example: A smart lock that requires a 3-digit ternary code to open, visualizing the sequence 0-1-2 as transitions between states.

sections.title: The Constrained Towers of Hanoi
sections.content: Introduce the 'Adjacent-Only' constraint: disks can only move to an adjacent peg. Explain how this restriction forces a sequence of moves that mimics a recursive pattern, mapping directly to ternary counting.
sections.example: A robot arm restricted to moving a disk only to the immediate left or right peg; show that moving a 3-disk tower requires exactly 3^n - 1 steps.

sections.title: Mapping Moves to the Sierpinski Triangle
sections.content: Visually map the sequence of legal moves in the constrained Hanoi puzzle onto the edges of a Sierpinski triangle. Each level of the triangle represents the state space of the disks.
sections.example: An animation of a disk-moving path that traces the perimeter of a growing Sierpinski fractal as the number of disks increases.

sections.title: Unified Synthesis & Conclusion
sections.content: Summarize how the ternary representation, the movement constraints, and the fractal geometry are isomorphic. The 'state' of the tower is simply a coordinate in a 2D fractal space.
sections.example: A final visual showing the 'Hanoi path' drawing the Sierpinski triangle in real-time, demonstrating that mathematics is just the discovery of these hidden structural symmetries.
